query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. Thin alloy diffusion barrier layers (DBnA, ∼7 nm) were prepared for examining their resistance to the interdiffusion of Cu and Si; thick alloy films (nA, 600–1000 nm) were for characterizing compositions, crystal structures and electrical resistivities. Sputtering targets were fabricated by arc-melting equimolar constituent elements in vacuum, and then cutting and polishing the solidified bulks into discs with a diameter of 50 mm. The thin barrier layers and thick alloy films were deposited on Si substrates at a radio-frequency power of 150 W and a substrate bias of −100 V, at room temperature, in an Ar atmosphere (gas flow rate of 30 sccm, working pressure of 6 × 10−3 torr). In the stage of corrosion, the material experiences an electrochemical effect that causes change or degradation of material, fundamentally into their oxides, aqueous salts or hydroxides. Accelerated immersion tests were conducted based on ASTM standard G34-0, before the HEA samples were subjected to an elevated temperature corrosive atmosphere. The corrosive solution used for these tests consisted of a mixture of 4 M NaCl, 0.5 M KNO3 and 0.1 M HNO3. The samples were kept in the corrosive solution for 5 days. All the elements in the HEAs composition were analyzed using an ICP-MS instrument (NexION 1000 ICP-MS, PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA) located at the University of Utah after diluting the solution by a factor of 10.
